title: The Song of the Reed
intro: Jalal al-Din Rumi (1207–1273), born in Balkh and settled in Konya in Anatolia, spent the last fifteen years of his life dictating the *Masnavi-ye Ma'navi* ('Spiritual Couplets') to his disciple Hosam al-Din Chalabi: six books and some 26,000 couplets of stories, teaching and jokes. Iranians call it simply the *Masnavi*, and its first eighteen couplets, the *Ney-nāme* or 'Song of the Reed', are the most famous lines in it. An old story says Rumi already had them written on a slip of paper in his turban when Hosam al-Din asked him for a book. The reed flute, the *ney*, was cut from its reed bed, and every note it plays is a lament for home; readers have always heard in it the soul, cut off from its source and longing to go back.

lines.fa: بشنو این نی چون شکایت می‌کند / از جدایی‌ها حکایت می‌کند
lines.r: beshnow in ney chon shekāyat mi-konad / az jodāyi-hā hekāyat mi-konad
lines.en: Listen to this reed, how it complains, / how it tells the story of separations.
lines.note: The best-known form of this line, quoted everywhere and printed in many popular editions, is «بشنو از نی چون حکایت می‌کند / از جدایی‌ها شکایت می‌کند» *beshnow az ney chon hekāyat mi-konad / az jodāyi-hā shekāyat mi-konad* – 'listen to the reed, how it tells its tale, / how it complains of separations'. Nicholson's edition, following the oldest manuscripts, has «بشنو این نی چون شکایت می‌کند», with 'complaint' and 'tale' the other way round.
words: listen! – imperative of شنیدن (today usually said beshno)
lines.faV: بِشنَو این نَی چون شِکایَت می‌کُنَد / اَز جُدایی‌ها حِکایَت می‌کُنَد

lines.fa: کز نیستان تا مرا ببریده‌اند / در نفیرم مرد و زن نالیده‌اند
lines.r: kaz neyestān tā marā bobride-and / dar nafir-am mard o zan nālide-and
lines.en: 'Ever since they cut me from the reed bed, / men and women have wept at my cry.'
lines.note: Some editions read «از نفیرم» *az nafir-am* 'at my cry'. From this couplet on, the reed itself is speaking.
words: they have cut (old ب- prefix + بریدن)
cry, wail; the blast of a horn
lines.faV: کَز نِیِستان تا مَرا بُبریده‌اَند / دَر نَفیرَم مَرد و زَن نالیده‌اَند

lines.fa: سینه خواهم شرحه شرحه از فراق / تا بگویم شرح درد اشتیاق
lines.r: sine khāham sharhe sharhe az ferāgh / tā beguyam sharh-e dard-e eshtiyāgh
lines.en: 'I want a breast torn to shreds by parting, / so that I can tell the pain of longing in full.'
lines.lit: a breast I want, strip by strip from separation, so that I tell the explanation of the pain of longing
lines.note: A play on two words that look alike: شرحه *sharhe* 'a strip of flesh' and شرح *sharh* 'a full account'.
words: I want – no می‌ in the classical present
lines.faV: سینه خواهَم شَرحه شَرحه اَز فِراق / تا بِگویَم شَرحِ دَردِ اِشتیاق

lines.fa: هر کسی کو دور ماند از اصل خویش / باز جوید روزگار وصل خویش
lines.r: har kasi ku dur mānd az asl-e khish / bāz juyad ruzgār-e vasl-e khish
lines.en: 'Whoever is left far from their origin / longs to find again the days of union.'
words: one's own – the same as خود
lines.faV: هَر کَسی کو دور ماند اَز اَصلِ خویش / باز جویَد روزگارِ وَصلِ خویش

lines.fa: من به هر جمعیتی نالان شدم / جفت بدحالان و خوش‌حالان شدم
lines.r: man be har jam'iyyati nālān shodam / joft-e bad-hālān o khosh-hālān shodam
lines.en: 'I have wept in every company; / I have kept company with the unhappy and the happy.'
lines.faV: مَن به هَر جَمعیَّتی نالان شُدَم / جُفتِ بَدحالان و خوش‌حالان شُدَم

lines.fa: هر کسی از ظن خود شد یار من / از درون من نجست اسرار من
lines.r: har kasi az zann-e khod shod yār-e man / az darun-e man najost asrār-e man
lines.en: 'Everyone became my friend through their own guesswork; / no one looked for the secrets within me.'
lines.faV: هَر کَسی اَز ظَنِّ خود شُد یارِ مَن / اَز دَرونِ مَن نَجُست اَسرارِ مَن

lines.fa: سر من از ناله‌ی من دور نیست / لیک چشم و گوش را آن نور نیست
lines.r: serr-e man az nāle-ye man dur nist / lik cheshm o gush rā ān nur nist
lines.en: 'My secret is not far from my lament, / but eye and ear do not have the light to find it.'
lines.faV: سِرِّ مَن اَز ناله‌یِ مَن دور نیست / لیک چِشم و گوش را آن نور نیست

lines.fa: تن ز جان و جان ز تن مستور نیست / لیک کس را دید جان دستور نیست
lines.r: tan ze jān o jān ze tan mastur nist / lik kas rā did-e jān dastur nist
lines.en: 'Body is not hidden from soul, nor soul from body, / yet no one is allowed to see the soul.'
words: from – the poetic short form of از
seeing, sight – the past stem used as a noun
lines.faV: تَن ز جان و جان ز تَن مَستور نیست / لیک کَس را دیدِ جان دَستور نیست

lines.fa: آتش است این بانگ نای و نیست باد / هر که این آتش ندارد نیست باد
lines.r: ātash ast in bāng-e nāy o nist bād / har ke in ātash nadārad nist bād
lines.en: 'This cry of the reed is fire, not wind; / whoever does not have this fire – may he be nothing!'
lines.note: Both halves end in the same two words, نیست باد, with two meanings: 'is not wind' and 'may he not be'. A rhyme on one word with two meanings is called جناس *jenās*.
words: reed flute – another form of نی
may he be nothing, may he perish
lines.faV: آتَش اَست این بانگِ نای و نیست باد / هَر که این آتَش نَدارَد نیست باد

lines.fa: آتش عشق است کاندر نی فتاد / جوشش عشق است کاندر می فتاد
lines.r: ātash-e 'eshgh ast kandar ney fetād / jushesh-e 'eshgh ast kandar mey fetād
lines.en: 'It is the fire of love that has fallen into the reed; / it is the ferment of love that has fallen into the wine.'
words: in, into – the old form of در
lines.faV: آتَشِ عِشق اَست کاَندَر نَی فِتاد / جوشِشِ عِشق اَست کاَندَر مَی فِتاد

lines.fa: نی حریف هر که از یاری برید / پرده‌هایش پرده‌های ما درید
lines.r: ney harif-e har ke az yāri borid / parde-hā-yash parde-hā-ye mā darid
lines.en: 'The reed is the companion of all who are cut off from a friend; / its melodies have torn away our veils.'
lines.note: پرده is both a curtain or veil and a note or mode in music: the reed's tunes tear away the veils we hide behind.
words: to be cut off from, to break with
curtain, veil; a mode or note in music
lines.faV: نَی حَریفِ هَر که اَز یاری بُرید / پَرده‌هایَش پَرده‌هایِ ما دَرید

lines.fa: همچو نی زهری و تریاقی که دید / همچو نی دمساز و مشتاقی که دید
lines.r: hamcho ney zahri o taryāghi ke did / hamcho ney damsāz o moshtāghi ke did
lines.en: 'Who ever saw a poison and an antidote like the reed? / Who ever saw a friend and a lover like the reed?'
words: who has seen? – a question expecting 'no one'
close friend, confidant – one who breathes in tune
lines.faV: هَمچو نَی زَهری و تَریاقی که دید / هَمچو نَی دَمساز و مُشتاقی که دید

lines.fa: نی حدیث راه پر خون می‌کند / قصه‌های عشق مجنون می‌کند
lines.r: ney hadis-e rāh-e por khun mi-konad / ghesse-hā-ye 'eshgh-e majnun mi-konad
lines.en: 'The reed tells of the road soaked in blood; / it tells the tales of Majnun's love.'
lines.note: Majnun, 'the possessed', is the madman of love whose story Nezami told in *Leyli and Majnun*.
words: mad, possessed – the lover of Leyli
lines.faV: نَی حَدیثِ راهِ پُر خون می‌کُنَد / قِصّه‌هایِ عِشقِ مَجنون می‌کُنَد

lines.fa: محرم این هوش جز بی‌هوش نیست / مر زبان را مشتری جز گوش نیست
lines.r: mahram-e in hush joz bi-hush nist / mar zabān rā moshtari joz gush nist
lines.en: 'Only the senseless are let into this sense, / just as the tongue has no buyer but the ear.'
lines.lit: the confidant of this mind is none but the mindless; for the tongue there is no buyer but the ear
words: an old way of marking 'for, to' or the object; مر adds no meaning
lines.faV: مَحرَمِ این هوش جُز بی‌هوش نیست / مَر زَبان را مُشتَری جُز گوش نیست

lines.fa: در غم ما روزها بیگاه شد / روزها با سوزها همراه شد
lines.r: dar gham-e mā ruz-hā bigāh shod / ruz-hā bā suz-hā hamrāh shod
lines.en: 'In our grief the days have grown late; / the days have gone hand in hand with burning.'
lines.note: The verbs are singular (شد) after the plural روزها: in classical Persian, things that are not people often take a singular verb.
lines.faV: دَر غَمِ ما روزها بیگاه شُد / روزها با سوزها هَمراه شُد

lines.fa: روزها گر رفت گو رو باک نیست / تو بمان ای آن که چون تو پاک نیست
lines.r: ruz-hā gar raft gu row bāk nist / to bemān ey ān ke chon to pāk nist
lines.en: 'If the days have gone, say: let them go, it does not matter – / only you remain, O you, the purest of all.'
lines.lit: the days, if they went, say 'go', there is no fear; you stay, O that one like whom none is pure
lines.faV: روزها گَر رَفت گو رَو باک نیست / تو بِمان اَی آن که چون تو پاک نیست

lines.fa: هر که جز ماهی ز آبش سیر شد / هر که بی‌روزیست روزش دیر شد
lines.r: har ke joz māhi ze āb-ash sir shod / har ke bi-ruzist ruz-ash dir shod
lines.en: 'All but the fish have had their fill of water; / whoever lacks his daily bread finds the day long.'
lines.note: روز 'day' and روزی 'daily bread' are another play on words. The fish is the true lover: it never has enough of the water it lives in.
words: of its water, of the water
to be full, to have had enough
is without his daily bread – بی‌روزی است
lines.faV: هَر که جُز ماهی ز آبَش سیر شُد / هَر که بی‌روزیست روزَش دیر شُد

lines.fa: در نیابد حال پخته هیچ خام / پس سخن کوتاه باید والسلام
lines.r: dar nayābad hāl-e pokhte hich khām / pas sokhan kutāh bāyad vas-salām
lines.en: 'No one raw can grasp the state of the ripe, / so the talk must be short – and that is all.'
words: to grasp, to understand – here split: در نیابد 'does not grasp'
any; with a negative verb, 'no one'
'and peace' (Arabic) – and that's that, end of story
lines.faV: دَر نَیابَد حالِ پُخته هیچ خام / پَس سُخَن کوتاه بایَد والسلام

commentary:
**The image.** The *ney*, the end-blown reed flute of Persian music, is cut from a reed bed, hollowed out and pierced, and it only sings when someone breathes into it. Rumi makes it the voice of every soul cut off from where it came from: its music is homesickness, and only those who have lost something hear what it is really saying. Notice how the speaker changes – Rumi asks us to listen in the first couplet, and from the second on the reed talks itself. Notice too the paradoxes: the reed is poison and cure; its song is fire, not wind; its 'mind' is open only to those who are out of their minds. In the last couplet Rumi breaks off: the raw cannot understand the cooked, so the talk must be short.

**The rhythm.** The whole *Masnavi* is in *ramal*, the metre of Attar's *Conference of the Birds*: three beats to the half-line, *DUM-da-DUM-DUM DUM-da-DUM-DUM DUM-da-DUM*. Read the first half-line slowly: *besh-na-vin ney chon she-kā-yat mi-ko-nad*. In a masnavi each couplet has its own rhyme – [[شکایت|shekāyat]] / [[حکایت|hekāyat]], [[فراق|ferāgh]] / [[اشتیاق|eshtiyāgh]] – which is why the form can run on for 26,000 couplets. Many couplets also repeat a word after the rhyme, as [[می‌کند|mi-konad]], [[شدم|shodam]] and [[نیست|nist]] do here.

**The grammar.** The language is easier than it looks. Watch for the run-together forms [[کز|kaz]] (که + از), [[کو|ku]] (که + او) and [[کاندر|kandar]] (که + اندر), for [[فتاد|fetād]] instead of [[افتاد|oftād]] and [[لیک|lik]] instead of [[لیکن|liken]], and for imperatives without [[ب|be-]]: [[گو|gu]] 'say', [[رو|row]] 'go'. The old word [[مر|mar]] in [[مر زبان را|mar zabān rā]] only strengthens [[را|rā]]. Couplet 4 in modern prose: [[هر کسی که از اصل خودش دور بماند، دوباره دنبال روزگار وصل خودش می‌گردد|har kasi ke az asl-e khod-ash dur bemānad, dobāre donbāl-e ruzgār-e vasl-e khod-ash mi-gardad]].

**Using it.** Recitals of the *Masnavi* begin with these lines, and singers and ney players have set them again and again. [[بشنو از نی|beshnow az ney]], in the popular reading, is a phrase in its own right. People quote [[هر کسی از ظن خود شد یار من|har kasi az zann-e khod shod yār-e man]] about friends who only see in us what they want to see, and [[پس سخن کوتاه باید والسلام|pas sokhan kutāh bāyad vas-salām]] to cut a long argument short.
